Battle of Fredericksburg. In December of eighteen sixty-two, Union General Ambrose E. Burnside sought to turn Lee's flank and capture Richmond. Instead, he led his army into a prepared defensive position where Robert E. Lee's Army of Northern Virginia held strong ground behind the town of Fredericksburg, Virginia. The Union launched repeated frontal assaults on the heights above the town, particularly Marye's Heights, and suffered catastrophic losses while inflicting comparatively light casualties on the defenders. The battle demonstrated the advantage of defensive entrenchment and led to Burnside's replacement as commander.

Burnside assumed command after Antietam and immediately sought to move aggressively toward Richmond. Lee repositioned his army to block the Union advance, selecting a strong defensive position behind the Rappahannock River. Union forces required pontoons to bridge the river, and Confederate artillery delayed their crossing.

Union forces crossed the river on December eleventh and cleared the town on December twelfth. Lee's main defensive line, anchored on Marye's Heights, was a stone wall at the base of an elevation where Confederate troops could fire at will on any attackers. On December thirteenth, Union divisions assaulted the heights in successive waves. Each assault was repulsed with heavy loss. More than twelve thousand Union soldiers fell in total, with six thousand of those casualties at the wall alone.

Burnside, despite urging from subordinates, pressed the attacks through December thirteenth. The Union withdrew across the river on December fifteenth. Total casualties showed the lopsided toll of the battle—approximately twelve thousand seven hundred for the Union against only six thousand for the Confederacy. This casualty ratio vindicated Confederate defensive tactics.

Fredericksburg was a triumphant moment for Lee and the Confederacy—one of the few battles where Union numerical superiority was negated by superior tactics and entrenchment. The repeated Union assaults on Marye's Heights became emblematic of the futility of frontal assault against prepared defensive positions, a lesson that would define World War I. For the Northern public, the defeat was demoralizing, but it also reinforced that the war would be decided through patience and attrition rather than brilliant maneuver. Lincoln replaced Burnside with Joseph "Fighting Joe" Hooker, seeking a commander more suited to modern warfare.
